heroByline: Produced By Ant Open Source & InclusionAI · September 2026
heroLede: Across 143 landscape projects, 100 high-activity repositories and 5,000 public Issues and pull requests, this report follows what changes when Agents join open-source development. The infrastructure map is filling in around runtimes, tools, isolation and evidence. On GitHub, Agents expand review and revision, but incoming code is growing faster than repositories can decide, integrate and maintain it.
mergeGateTitle: Agents are working inside the repository
mergeGateBody: Agents read contribution rules, edit files, run tests and respond to review. That puts them inside the ordinary Issue and pull-request loop. The question is whether they shorten the path to a useful change or mainly increase the volume that maintainers have to judge.
executionGateTitle: Agents bring code to the runtime
executionGateBody: An agent may write code after a task has started, open a browser, call internal services and keep state across several short-lived environments. Infrastructure has to isolate work it has never seen before, limit the authority of each task and preserve enough evidence to explain what changed after the process is gone.
landscapeOverviewTitle: Agent applications lead the activity. Runtime is where the landscape is filling in.
landscapeOverviewBody: The current landscapes contain 84 Agent Infra and 59 Model Infra projects. Applications hold 55% of Agent Infra's July OpenRank, while Runtime accounts for 13 of the 23 Agent Infra selections outside the May tracking pool. Model Infra remains an older, Python-led systems base, with Serving holding 44% of its July OpenRank. The map shows both where activity sits and where production responsibilities are accumulating.
landscapeTitle: Applications hold the activity. Runtime holds more of the new selections.
agentChartTitle: Attention is still concentrated at the application layer
modelChartTitle: Serving still carries the systems weight
ageFinding: Most Agent Infra projects were created during the current wave. The serving engines, schedulers and data systems underneath them are older, and now have to carry short-lived code, delegated tool access and state that outlives a process.
languageTitle: Agent products lean TypeScript. Model infrastructure still speaks Python.
languageBody: GitHub identifies TypeScript as the primary language in 33 of 84 Agent Infra repositories, while Python leads 33 of 59 Model Infra repositories. The contrast fits the shape of the two maps: more web-facing products on the Agent side, and more model-serving and systems work underneath. The Other category includes Rust, Java, Shell and smaller languages.
runtimePathTitle: Runtime projects are clustering along the path an agent takes through a task.
runtimePathBody: The map is filling in around context, interfaces, tool execution, isolation and evidence. These categories connect the project landscape to the task now reaching Kubernetes, OpenInfra, workload identity and telemetry systems.
growthSummary: From April to July, the six largest OpenRank gains came from projects working on tool use, context and inference efficiency. OpenRank follows repository activity, so the pattern points to the parts of the open-source stack attracting more contributors and discussion.
outsideGithubTitle: The same workload is visible beyond repository activity.
outsideGithubBody: Nine of OpenRouter’s opt-in global Top 20 apps on 29 August map directly to Agent Infra projects, including seven of the Top 10. A separate ZenMux snapshot for 1–30 June shows heavy use of model endpoints tied to public-weight repositories. These two platform views echo the same demand visible in the landscape: agent applications are generating traffic, while open models remain part of the delivery path.
collaborationTitle: PR intake doubled. Review and integration did not keep pace.
collaborationLede: The same 55 repositories received 105% more pull requests than in 2025. Named Agents appeared in more threads and more PRs reached review, but first-week maintainer response and 30-day PR completion both fell. This chapter follows that widening gap: how much work arrived, where Agents contributed and who still carried a change through the final public action.
collaborationProfileBody: We froze the 100 highest-July-OpenRank repositories in the 277-project tracking pool, then reviewed every project for its technical role and relationship to LLMs. This activity-led view describes prominent projects in the tracked ecosystem; smaller and quieter repositories sit outside it.
collaborationAdoptionTitle: Coding-agent setup is already common across the stack.
collaborationAdoptionBody: We found an instruction file or tool folder in 92 of the Top 100 repositories. Coverage is high in every technical group, so the more useful question is no longer whether repositories are preparing for coding agents, but what happens when Agent-assisted work reaches the public contribution process.
collaborationTasksTitle: Agent activity clusters around review and triage.
collaborationTasksBody: Across the 5,000 sampled threads, named Agents produced 5,363 review events, 1,915 discussion comments and 1,448 triage or routing events. We found only 87 Agent-opened threads and 114 publicly attributed commits. The visible workload is concentrated after a contribution arrives, where repositories already spend time checking, routing and responding.
collaborationEntryTitle: Agents mostly join after a contribution arrives.
collaborationEntryBody: Only 87 of the 5,000 sampled threads were opened by a named Agent or App. Agent review was much more common: it appeared on 1,342 of 3,567 pull requests. At the other end of the workflow, a GitHub User account performed the final visible merge, close or reopen action in 88.5% of resolved threads.
collaborationIterationTitle: An Agent-first review is more often followed by another commit.
collaborationIterationBody: Among reviewed pull requests, another commit followed 66.8% of Agent-first reviews and 41.1% of User-first reviews. Explicit change requests sharpen the picture: 76.5% of Agent requests and 77.4% of User requests were followed by another commit. Agent review is already part of the revision loop; the clearest signal of another round is a concrete request to change the code.
collaborationLineageTitle: The first Agent patch often survives—and sometimes gets rewritten.
collaborationLineageBody: We followed ten merged pull requests in which a verified Coding Agent changed the code, then carried every line from the first effective Agent patch through the later commits. Nine PRs expose a clean line history: 765 of 1,225 lines remain unchanged, 123 are first changed by a User-account commit and 193 by a later Agent commit. The cases include Agent-only revision, Agent-to-human hand-offs and patches that survive unchanged.
collaborationGovernanceTitle: Most repositories accept outside pull requests. A smaller group asks contributors to align first.
collaborationGovernanceBody: Ninety-eight of the Top 100 let anyone create a pull request; Codex and Claude Code restrict creation to collaborators. Twelve repositories keep PR creation open but ask contributors to open an Issue, seek approval or stay within a defined scope before coding. DeepSeek Harness, outside the Top 100, shows a sharper boundary: public code, closed core contribution and an open plugin path.
collaborationBurdenTitle: The Agent era expanded the flow of code. The merge path did not speed up with it.
collaborationBurdenBody: Across the same 55 repositories, PR intake rose from 129,563 in 2025 to 265,447 in 2026. Ninety days after arrival, the share still open rose from 5.5% to 11.3%, while the repository-median merge rate fell from 77.0% to 68.4%. The thread timelines below show where human response and revision fit inside that widening gap.
collaborationScarcityTitle: Outside contributors supply most pull requests. User accounts still perform the final public action.
collaborationScarcityBody: External accounts opened 66.8% of the 3,567 sampled pull requests, and a named Agent reviewed 37.6% of them. Among 4,089 resolved threads, a GitHub User account performed the last visible merge, close or reopen action in 88.5%. Intake and review are distributed widely; changing the repository’s public state remains concentrated in User accounts.
caseTitle: The contribution surface sits outside the core repository
caseQuote: “You may consider this repository an idea, an official showcase, and a source of inspiration, but not a mandate from us.”
caseBody: The project treats its official code as a reference point and third-party plugins as the place where the ecosystem can branch out. That arrangement leaves practical governance work around interface stability, discovery and what happens when a plugin becomes unsafe or abandoned.
governanceInterface: Interface stability needs a visible owner.
governanceDiscovery: Plugin discovery needs verification and provenance.
governanceRevocation: Unsafe or abandoned capabilities need a revocation path.
studyTitle: How the collaboration evidence fits together
studyNote: All 2026 collaboration measures stop at 31 August. The repository scan covers all 100 projects. The thread analysis follows 50 Issues or pull requests from each repository and links their reviews, comments, commits and state changes through that date. Every sampled thread counts once. Actor labels follow the identity GitHub exposes, so User describes an account type while named Agent and App actions are counted separately.
infrastructureTitle: Agent execution is variable, stateful and capable of side effects.
infrastructureLede: A task can generate code after it starts, fan out across model and tool calls, pause, retry and leave a change behind. Platform token totals combine many such runs and hide their peaks, waits and retries. Infrastructure therefore has to keep isolation, authority, budget, state and evidence attached to the task while individual processes come and go.
infrastructureProjectTitle: Open projects cover much of the path. The gaps sit between them.
infrastructureProjectBody: Some projects were built for agents. Others bring mature isolation, identity, scheduling and tracing into the task. The remaining work is task-wide: budgets, cancellation, safe recovery and evidence still stop at component boundaries.
closingQuestion: Agents expand the supply of patches. Open source still has to decide what a project can absorb and maintain.
closingNote: The evidence points to a real gain in review and revision capacity, but not a matching gain in integration. In the Agent era, contribution is not simply producing more code. It is connecting a change to a shared problem, carrying it through review and leaving a community willing to own what remains.
